topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Let two related dimensions change independently instead of building a separate subclass for every combination. Worked example: Counts in plain text and brackets. Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Separate two independent reasons a class family changes.
Trace calls across a report-to-writer bridge.
Add an output format without changing reporting rules.

blocks.text: An Abstraction offers the operation the application needs and holds a connection to an Implementation interface. Refined Abstractions change high-level behavior. Concrete Implementations supply lower-level operations. Construction selects the pairing; ordinary calls cross the stored connection. These are pattern roles, not synonyms for the C++ words abstract class and implementation file. The attached Abstraction can be instantiated even though its role is called Abstraction.

cards.question: What problem does Bridge address?
cards.answer: Let two related dimensions change independently instead of building a separate subclass for every combination. Worked example: Counts in plain text and brackets. Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit.

cards.question: What is Bridge?
cards.answer: A connection that lets a high-level operation and its implementation vary independently.

cards.question: What is Variation dimension?
cards.answer: One independent kind of change, such as report meaning or output format.

cards.question: What is Cross-product?
cards.answer: The set of every pairing from two sets of choices.

cards.question: Must the Abstraction and Implementation declare identical operations?
cards.answer: No. The abstraction may combine lower-level operations. Report chooses a label; Writer only formats the supplied label and number.

cards.question: What demonstrates Bridge more strongly than merely storing a Writer pointer?
cards.answer: Both report meanings work with both formats, and adding a format requires no changes to those report meanings. The independent dimensions are observable.

cards.question: Why are CountCsv and WarningCsv subclasses unnecessary?
cards.answer: The report supplies meaning and delegates representation to Writer. Csv can be paired with both existing report types without multiplying combined subclasses.

cards.question: What lifetime condition must hold for a Report constructed from a Writer reference?
cards.answer: The writer must remain alive for every report call. Constructing a report from a temporary writer and retaining it would leave a dangling borrow.

cards.question: Is Bridge the same as converting milligrams to grams?
cards.answer: No. Adapter repairs a mismatch with an existing interface. This Bridge separates report meaning from formatting so both dimensions can grow independently.

cards.question: Where should a new warning threshold be implemented?
cards.answer: In report policy, not Csv or Brackets. Writers receive an already chosen label and number and should not decide when a count is high.

cards.question: Would a function parameter for formatting be simpler?
cards.answer: Often yes, if the behavior is small and the report does not need a persistent polymorphic interface. Bridge describes the separation, not a requirement to maximize classes.

cards.question: Why test one writer with two report kinds?
cards.answer: It checks that the new representation composes with existing meanings. Testing only one combination may miss a hard-coded label or special case.

cards.question: Does sharing a const Writer reference guarantee thread safety?
cards.answer: No general guarantee follows from const alone. A concrete writer could use mutable state or external resources; its implementation must supply any concurrency guarantee.

topics.title: Two useful reports, two useful formats
topics.summary: A small inspection tool prints a count and also classifies that count. One screen wants count=6. Another wants [count:6]. The classification report calls counts above five high and all others normal. It must work in either format. Negative counts are invalid. Requirements now vary in two directions: what the report means, and how its fields are written.

blocks.text: The simplest first version returns a string directly from a function. That is a good solution when there is one meaning and one format. A second function can serve a second fixed report. The difficulty appears when both dimensions grow. If each combination has its own class, two report types and two formats need four combinations. Three types and four formats need twelve. The count is the product of the choices, not automatically an exponential function of one choice. What hurts is repeated policy and repeated formatting.

discussion.question: How many combinations arise from two report meanings and two output formats? What changes when a third format is added?
discussion.answer: There are four combinations, then six. Writing a subclass for every combination duplicates policy and formatting. The next step separates the two choices so they can be combined.

topics.title: Locate the two decisions before drawing classes
topics.summary: Suppose the warning boundary changes from five to ten. In the combined design, each warning-format class must change. Suppose the bracket screen changes its separator. Every bracket-report class must change. That gives a concrete reason to separate the decisions. The boundary rule belongs with the report; punctuation belongs with the writer. Neither side should inspect the exact type on the other side.

blocks.text: A bridge is a stable connection between a high-level operation and a lower-level implementation that can vary independently. Here Report supplies the high-level render operation and borrows a Writer. CountReport and WarningReport decide which field name to send. Plain and Brackets implement Writer::field. The bridge is the writer_ reference. The two families can now grow without adding one class for every cross-product combination.

The pattern's traditional word abstraction means the high-level view offered to the caller. It does not require every high-level class to be an abstract C++ base class. Our Report is abstract because two report meanings already exist and both must be usable through the same contract. A single concrete report with a Writer member would still separate format from meaning when only one report is needed.

topics.title: Trace data and control across the bridge
topics.summary: In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them. cp stores a reference to plain; cb stores a reference to brackets. Calling cb.render(6) enters CountReport. validate first rejects a negative value. The report then sends the label count and integer 6 to writer_.field. Virtual dispatch selects Brackets::field. It creates [count:6] and returns that string by value through the report to main.

blocks.text: WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first. The conditional expression n > 5 ? "high" : "normal" evaluates the condition, selects exactly one of the two strings, and initializes label. The question mark introduces the true result, and the colon separates it from the false result. This colon is different from the colon that begins a constructor initializer list or a range loop. Syntax takes its meaning from its surrounding statement.

The returned strings own their character storage. The label passed to field is a const reference, so field borrows the argument during the call. Neither writer keeps that reference afterward. writer_ is a longer-lived borrow stored inside Report. Those are different lifetime obligations: a call parameter need only stay valid for the call, while a stored reference must stay valid for later calls too.

topics.title: What compilation guarantees and what it cannot
topics.summary: The compiler checks public inheritance, virtual signatures, and whether each concrete class implements the required operation. override catches a mismatch. protected makes writer_ and validate available to the derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. The helper is static because it depends only on its argument and needs no Report object. Constructors initialize the reference before any render call can occur.

blocks.text: The compiler does not verify that a new Writer preserves the label and value faithfully. A writer could accidentally swap field names or drop a minus sign. That would still compile. The shared semantic contract is therefore essential: format the supplied name and integer without changing their meaning. The report checks the domain rule that counts cannot be negative. The generic writer is capable of formatting any integer, which makes it usable in other domains.

At execution the same report can use either writer selected during construction. Our design does not provide a setter to switch writer_ later; C++ references cannot be rebound. To change format, construct a new report borrowing another writer. This keeps ownership and configuration simple. An application needing live format changes could instead hold a non-owning pointer with an explicit non-null rule or own an interchangeable writer. That requirement has not appeared here, so its extra states are unnecessary.

topics.title: When the split helps, and when it does not
topics.summary: A bridge gives independence only when the interface is stable and truthful. If field lacks data one format needs, reports may begin checking for special writers. That is a warning that the boundary is too narrow or the supposedly independent dimensions are actually linked. Improve the contract using a real use case, or accept a smaller set of supported combinations. Do not promise that every conceivable report will work with every renderer.

blocks.text: An enum and one formatting function may be smaller when the set of formats is fixed and tiny. A template can select a writer at compilation and may remove virtual calls, but it exposes more implementation to callers and moves the choice from runtime to build time. Neither alternative is inherently inferior. The reason for this bridge is the already demonstrated independent growth in report policy and presentation.

Bridge and Adapter can produce similar shapes in a diagram. Their motivations differ. An adapter repairs an existing disagreement between interfaces. A bridge deliberately separates dimensions that should evolve independently. When reviewing a change, ask what boundary is being protected. Add tests for each report's meaning and each format's text, plus a few combinations. That protects the separation more effectively than checking only class names.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: The threshold belongs to the report and must remain the same across formats. A writer may reject a label it cannot encode, such as unsupported control characters, if its contract documents that restriction. It should not silently change the label or numeric meaning.

workshop.title: Counts in plain text and brackets
workshop.problem: Counts in plain text and brackets. Support count and warning reports in both formats. Classify n > 5 as high; zero through five as normal. Reject negative counts before formatting.

steps.why: main selects the pairing during construction.
The report owns the meaning decision.
The report threshold is strictly greater than five.

workshop.pitfall: Duplicate the warning threshold in every writer. One format may print high for 6 while another prints normal. A domain rule has been scattered across format implementations.

discussion.question: There will always be exactly one report and two formats selected at compile time. Compare a bridge with two formatting helper functions.
discussion.answer: Two helpers may be clearer and avoid inheritance. A bridge becomes attractive when multiple reports and independently added runtime writers appear. A template is another reasonable choice if selection stays at compile time and code size remains acceptable.
discussion.hint: Look for demonstrated independent growth and selection time.

workshop.alternative: An enum-based formatter is simpler for a permanently closed set of formats. Templates fit compile-time selection; virtual writers fit objects selected while the program runs.
workshop.design: Two report types share a Writer interface because report policy and field formatting change for different reasons. Constructors make each pairing explicit.
invariants: Reports never change a writer or own its lifetime.
Writers preserve the supplied name and numeric value.
workshop.maintenance: Adding a screen format should modify its Writer implementation and construction site. A report-policy change should remain in the report family.
workshop.verification: All four combinations are checked for six, plus the threshold five, zero, and a negative rejected case. These checks establish the example contract, not arbitrary escaping rules or performance.
